en: Since Your greatness is infinite, any praise for You by one who knows even the highest truths would be inadequate;

thus, even the words of Brahmā and the other gods fall short when directed toward You. Furthermore, if one were to speak only until the limit of one's own intellectual capacity, then everything remains unspeakable. Yet, one who praises You in this manner is truly praising You.
O Hara, this very preparation for my hymn is also free from fault:
your majesty has transcended the path of both speech and mind,
and even the Veda describes it with trepidation by means of the exclusion of what it is not.
By whom is he to be praised? Of how many kinds are his qualities? To whom is he the object?
For whose mind does it not fall upon his lower state, and for whose speech does it not fail?
[He is the one] who fashioned the supreme nectar of words, rich with the sweetness of honey.
O Brahmin, what indeed could even the speech of the Preceptor of the Gods be that would cause you wonder?
However, with the merit of praising your virtues, my mind is resolved upon this purpose: "I shall purify myself by means of these words of yours," O Destroyer of Cities.

O Giver of Boons, that sovereignty of Yours which effects the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the universe— manifested as the three Vedas within Your three bodies distinguished by the [three] qualities—
is delightful to some, yet repulsive to those who lack fortune.
Some here, of dull intellect, utter insults in order to refute [this]:
"With what desire, with what body, by what means, and supported by what, does the Creator create the three worlds; and what is the material cause?"

In You, whose sovereign power is beyond reasoning, this faulty logic of those with ruined intellects—standing ill at ease due to its untimeliness—makes certain people clamor for the sake of deluding the world:
"Are the worlds unborn, even though they possess parts? [Smṛti 5]
Does the law of existence proceed without disregarding a presiding director?
Or, being powerless, how could it create the world? For what purpose [would such power be needed], since these dull-witted ones, O best of immortals, thus doubt regarding you?

The Vedic triple canon, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the doctrine of Paśupati, and that of Viṣṇu— these are the various divergent systems; and among those who follow straight or crooked paths of many kinds due to the diversity of their inclinations, each claims, "This is the supreme [truth], this is the beneficial."
To men you alone are approachable, like the ocean is to the waters.
O Giver of Boons, these are your ritual implements: a great bull, a skull-topped staff, an axe, a deerskin, ashes, serpents, and a human skull.
The gods indeed possess various supernatural powers when directed by Your brow,
for the mirage of sense-objects does not delude one who delights in the Self.
Surely, one [sees] all as eternal, while another sees this entire world as impermanent.
O Destroyer of Tripura, another speaks of permanence and impermanence regarding the world when its objects are considered individually;
yet, O Destroyer of Tripura, even when these two are taken together, I am as if struck with wonder and hesitate to praise you— though indeed, such boldness in speech is not truly audacious.
O Giriśa, since even Viriñca above and Hari below were unable to fully measure the extent of your sovereignty despite their efforts— each possessing a body with shoulders as vast as fire—
it is for this reason that we two, burdened by the weight of devotion and faith, offer our praise.

Since the Ten-faced one, having effortlessly brought the three worlds under his sway without any conflict, bore arms that were overcome by the itch for battle, why does your compliance with those two not bear fruit? You yourself remained standing by them. Why does your devotion not yield its reward?
O Destroyer of Tripura, this is the manifestation of your firm devotion, which has gained strength from the lotus-feet of the Lord whose head is adorned by a row of lotuses;
for his forest of arms has acquired its essence through service to you.
Even as he forcibly attempted to display his prowess upon Kailāsa, your own abode,
his very foothold became unattainable— even in Pātāla— since the tip of his big toe remained motionless; yet it is certain that a wicked man becomes deluded when he has grown powerful.

That Bāṇa— who held the three worlds under his command through his attendants— brought even the exceedingly lofty supernatural power of Sutrāman down to earth is not surprising, given that he was a worshiper of your feet.

O Three-eyed One, your bowing before him— who was moved by compassion for the gods and asuras terrified by the sudden destruction of the universe, and who had swallowed the poison— does not lead to the exaltation of anyone’s head.

The dark spot on your throat brings no beauty; yet, oh, even such a blemish is praiseworthy for one who is devoted to destroying the fear of the world! For nowhere among gods, asuras, or humans has there ever been anyone whose purpose remained unfulfilled.
O Lord, seeing you— who are common to all other gods— the victorious arrows of Smara constantly turn back in this world; for indeed,
when one's very self is to be remembered, humiliation is not beneficial toward those who possess self-mastery.
The earth suddenly falls into a state of peril from the strike of his feet;

the sky repeatedly suffers distress as its surface is struck by his wildly tossing matted locks, while the host of planets is crushed by his whirling, club-like arms— [all this occurring] at every step of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, your power alone is wondrous as you dance for the protection of the world!
That stream of water which pervades the sky, its beauty enhanced by the foam produced by the clusters of stars, is seen upon your head as a mere spray.

By this very fact— that the world, shaped like an island and encircled by the ocean, was fashioned by you— it is to be inferred that your divine body possesses sustained majesty. The earth is the chariot, Śatadhṛti (Brahmā) is the driver, and the king of mountains is the bow.
The two wheels of the chariot are the moon and the sun, and the one with the discus in hand is the arrow.
O you who desire to burn them, what is this display of grandeur toward Tripura, which is but straw?
Indeed, the intellects of lords do not play while being dependent on others.
When Hari, having placed a thousand lotus offerings at your feet, offered his own lotus-eye as the one remaining in that set,
that excess of devotion reached its full fruition in the form of the Cakravartin.
O Destroyer of Tripura, you remain awake for the protection of the three worlds;
while the sacrifice sleeps, you are awake to bestow the fruit upon those who perform it.
Where does an action once destroyed ever reappear, except through the propitiation of the Supreme Person?
Therefore, beholding you as the guarantor for the granting of fruits in the sacrifices,
people— having established faith in the sacred revelation and girding themselves firmly for ritual acts— perform them;
you who are skilled in action, Dakṣa, Lord of Sacrifice, and Sovereign of embodied beings.
O Giver of Refuge, the seers performed the office of the officiating priests and the hosts of gods served as the members of the assembly; yet,
for you— who are devoted to the prescription of the fruits of sacrifice— the failure of the rite was certain, for the sacrifices of a performer devoid of faith lead only to malevolent magic.
He who, having violently pursued his own daughter who had become a doe,
desiring to sport with her in the form of a stag,
went even to heaven while bow in hand, though he was struck down by arrows.
O Destroyer of Cities, even now the impetuous hunter of deer does not abandon him who is trembling,
having seen even the Flower-Armed God— whose bow was strung with the hope of his own beauty— immediately consumed before him like a blade of grass.

O Giver of Boons, O Destroyer of Smara, if young women— deluded by their devotion to the female sex— should truly recognize you through your union with half of your own body as one intent on restraint, alas!
Their playgrounds would be the cremation grounds and their companions would be ghouls.
Though your practice consists of smearing yourself with funeral ashes, wearing garlands made of human skulls,
and maintaining an inauspicious demeanor— let all this be as it may—
nevertheless, O Giver of Boons, you are the supreme auspiciousness for those who remember you.
Having fixed their minds within the inner consciousness,
having restrained their breath, with hair standing on end and eyes bathed in tears of joy,
they beheld that [bliss] which, like plunging into a lake of nectar, fills them with delight.
It is said that the self-restrained hold within them some ineffable reality; and that, indeed, is you.
You are the sun, you are the moon, you are the wind, you are the fire, you are the waters, you are the ether, and you are the earth; you are the Self.
Thus, we do not know that ultimate reality which you do not possess here, even though they bear speech toward you as something merely circumscribed— namely,
the three Vedas, the three modes of conduct, the three worlds, and even the three gods.

O Giver of Refuge, this word "iti" praises You— the Fourth State who has transcended all transformation— expressing Your abode through the three letters beginning with *na*, which, by means of subtle sounds, encompass You both collectively and individually.
O Lord, even the Veda itself applies each of these eight names— Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Paśupati, Ugra, Mahādeva, Bhīma, and Īśāna—
to You individually.
I offer my salutation to you, who have been prostrated before for the sake of this beloved abode. Salutations to the nearest and salutations to the most distant;
salutations to the smallest, O destroyer of Smara, and salutations to the greatest.
Homage to the most ancient and to the youngest, the three-eyed one; homage, repeated homage, to you who are all, to this very world, and to the All;
homage to Bhava, who possesses abundant passion for the creation of the universe.
Salutations again and again to Hara, who brings about the destruction of that most intense darkness;

salutations again and again to Mṛda, who creates the world of beings for the sake of the happiness of people; salutations again and again to Śiva, who abides in the state of supreme splendor beyond the three qualities (guṇas).

"Where is this mind of mine, emaciated in its development and subject to the afflictions, and where is your eternal increase that transcends the limits of all virtues?"— having thus caused me to rejoice despite my trepidation, devotion has established me [in you].
And offer at your feet this tribute of flowers that are my words.
*Pariśiṣṭa*: Additional verses found in all manuscripts.
But it is not so in the inscription:
"Collyrium equal to the Asita mountain [in quantity], with the ocean as its vessel, the branch of the best of celestial trees as the pen, and the earth as the leaf..."
O Lord, even if Śāradā were to write down your qualities at all times while holding her pen, she would still not reach their end—
you who are worshipped by the lords of the asuras, the gods, and the sages, and who bear the crescent moon upon your crest.

Puṣpadanta, the most eminent among all those possessing virtuous qualities, composed this beautiful hymn in long metrical verses for the Lord, whose greatness of virtues is renowned, yet who is himself devoid of [material] qualities.
That man of pure heart who recites this faultless hymn to Dhūrjaṭi with supreme devotion day after day becomes,
in the world of Śiva, equal to Rudra himself, possessing the nature of the eternal Self.
One will possess abundant wealth, long life, sons, and fame.
(Smṛtyaddhyāya 3) There is no god greater than Maheśa; there is no hymn of praise greater than Mahiman;
there is no mantra greater than Aghora; and there is no reality higher than that of the Guru. (Smṛtyaddhyāya 4)
Initiation, charity, austerity, pilgrimage, knowledge, and rituals such as sacrifices—
these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of reciting your majesty.
This meritorious hymn, spoken by the Gandharva, remains complete.
The description of the Lord is incomparable, captivating, and auspicious. Kusumadaśana, the king of all the Gandharvas,
is a servant of the God of gods, who bears the young moon upon his crest.
Indeed, fallen from his own majesty through his anger,
he performed this most divine hymn of "Majesty" (Mahimnaḥ-stava),
having worshipped the Teacher of the Gods, the sole cause of heaven and liberation.
If a person recites this unfailing hymn composed by Puṣpadanta with palms joined in reverence and undistracted mind, they go into the presence of Śiva while being praised by the kinnaras.
By this hymn— which issues from the lotus-like mouth of Śrī Puṣpadanta, which removes all sins, and is beloved by Hara—
the Great Lord Maheśa, the Master of Beings, becomes thoroughly pleased when it is kept at the throat, recited, or kept in the home.
As they contemplate your unprecedented beauty, your body is divested of its garments.
An extraordinary bond arose between the sages and their wives,
such that even if the secret [of their union] were revealed once,
it would surely produce liberation for those who perform worship, as well as some divine play and the supreme human goal.
From the manifestation of this body, O Enemy of Tripura, I have inferred that in my previous births I never once prostrated before you.
Having now prostrated, I am liberated; being bodiless, I shall remain free from pride even in the future.
"O Maheśa, may even these two offenses of mine be forgiven.
Thus is this worship consisting of speech offered at the feet of the illustrious Śaṅkara;
may Sadāśiva, the Lord of Gods, be pleased with me.
I do not know your true nature; what you are, O Maheśvara, such as you are, O Mahādeva, to you I offer salutation after salutation. That man who recites this once, twice, or thrice a day—
Freed from the long noose, he goes to the world of Śiva.
Indeed, by the chanting of Rudra’s name, sin is shattered into a thousand pieces,
just as a mass of clouds is dispersed by a fierce wind.
